overview: Edmontosaurus regalis and E. annectens were among the largest hadrosaurs, reaching 12–13 metres and up to 4 tonnes, from the latest Cretaceous of North America (~73–66 Ma). A remarkable "Edmontosaurus mummy" — with extensive skin and soft-tissue preservation including a fleshy crest on the head — provided unprecedented detail about hadrosaur integument and revealed a cock's-comb-like structure not visible in the skeleton alone.

Edmontosaurus was the most abundant large herbivore at the very end of the Cretaceous, sharing its world with Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops. Bite marks on Edmontosaurus tail vertebrae from a large tyrannosaur — and a healed tail that shows the animal survived the attack — provide direct evidence of sublethal predator-prey interaction between T. rex and its most common prey.

articles.title: The mummies
articles.body: At least three Edmontosaurus specimens preserve extensive skin and soft tissue — more than any other non-avian dinosaur genus. The most complete (AMNH 5060, "Trachodon mummy") was collected by Charles Sternberg's sons in 1908 and shows desiccated skin, tendons and the impression of a fleshy crest on the skull. A 2013 specimen revealed a rounded cock's-comb-like structure on the head, completely invisible in skeletal material.

articles.title: T. rex predation evidence
articles.body: A tail vertebra of Edmontosaurus bears a puncture wound matching large tyrannosaur tooth size, and the surrounding bone shows extensive healing — the hadrosaur survived. This is the clearest published example of a sublethal T. rex attack on a large herbivore and confirms that T. rex did actively hunt healthy prey rather than only scavenge.

articles.title: Hadrosaur dental batteries
articles.body: Edmontosaurus had hundreds of teeth arranged in a grinding battery — up to 60 teeth stacked in each position with replacements developing below. This system could efficiently process the tough conifer vegetation of the Late Cretaceous. The grinding surface produced by the battery resembles a millstone in function, processing large volumes of plant material rapidly.

record.mya: late Campanian-early Maastrichtian, roughly 73-69 million years ago for E. regalis
record.description: Edmontosaurus regalis was a large, broad-beaked saurolophine hadrosaurid from the Horseshoe Canyon and equivalent formations of Canada. Numerous skulls and skeletons across growth stages document its anatomy; later Maastrichtian E. annectens is a separate species and should not be blended into one undifferentiated profile.
facts: Multiple specimens preserve skin impressions, and one Edmontosaurus specimen preserves a fleshy head comb.
Dental batteries and wear surfaces document sophisticated plant processing.
It could move both quadrupedally and bipedally; habitual speed and herd structure are not directly known.

review.ageReviewNote: The profile is scoped to E. regalis, primarily about 73-69 Ma; E. annectens extends the genus into the latest Maastrichtian but is taxonomically distinct.

residualUncertainty: Some historic specimens and formations require species-level reassignment.
